title: Review: Carbon compounds as fuels and feedstock

Clues: 4.7.1-c14 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.7.1-c03 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.7.1-c17 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.7.1-c18 first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.7.1-q03, 4.7.1-q13, 4.7.1-q10, 4.7.1-q14, 4.7.1-q01, 4.7.1-q11, 4.7.1-q02, 4.7.1-q17, 4.7.1-q07, 4.7.1-q12, 4.7.1-q08, 4.7.1-q16. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Evaporation
items.clue: Turning a liquid into a vapour.

items.label: Condensation
items.clue: Turning a vapour back into a liquid.

options.text: A molecule made of hydrogen, carbon and oxygen atoms
Any compound that contains carbon in its molecules
A molecule made of hydrogen and carbon atoms only
Any substance that burns to release energy

questions.explanation: The specification defines hydrocarbons as molecules made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.

questions.stem: How does fractional distillation separate the hydrocarbons in crude oil?

options.text: The oil is melted, then each fraction freezes out at a different temperature
The oil is filtered, and the larger molecules are held by a fine mesh
The oil is burned, and the gases given off are then collected separately
The oil is evaporated, then each fraction condenses at a different temperature

questions.explanation: Evaporation followed by condensation at different heights in the column is exactly how the specification requires this to be explained.

questions.stem: Which of these substances is an alkane?

options.text: C₅H₁₀ — hydrogen atoms = 2 × 5 exactly
C₅H₁₂O — it has 12 hydrogen atoms
C₄H₈ — it is also a hydrocarbon
C₅H₁₂ — hydrogen atoms = 2 × 5 + 2

questions.explanation: It fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 5, so it is an alkane.

questions.stem: Why are the fractions containing the largest molecules collected near the bottom of the column?

options.text: They have the highest boiling points, so they condense first
The bottom of the fractionating column is the coolest part of it
They are the densest, so they sink down to the bottom
They have the lowest boiling points of all fractions

questions.explanation: The column is hottest at the bottom, so the fractions with the highest boiling points condense there.

questions.stem: Crude oil is found in rocks. What was crude oil formed from?

options.text: The remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton
The remains of dinosaurs and other large animals buried in mud
The remains of ancient forests of land plants buried in swamp
Minerals in the rock that were changed by heat and pressure

questions.explanation: This is exactly what the specification states: crude oil is the remains of an ancient biomass, mainly plankton, buried in mud.

questions.stem: Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation. What is the separation based on?

options.text: Differences in the boiling points of the molecules
Differences in how fast the molecules react together
Differences in the density of the liquid hydrocarbons
Differences in the colours of the compounds

questions.explanation: Fractional distillation sorts hydrocarbons by the temperature at which their vapour condenses, which depends on boiling point.

questions.stem: Why is crude oil described as a finite resource?

options.text: New oil is forming at the same rate that we use it
New crude oil forms far more slowly than we use it up
It is only found in a small number of countries on Earth
It is a mixture, so it cannot be put together again

questions.explanation: A finite resource is one being consumed much faster than it is replaced, so supplies will run out.

questions.stem: Which of these are produced by the petrochemical industry?

options.text: Solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents
Petrol, diesel oil, kerosene and fuel oil
Limestone, cement, sand and glass items
Nitrogen, oxygen and argon, taken from air

questions.explanation: These are the four examples of useful materials the specification gives for the petrochemical industry.

questions.stem: What are the first four members of the alkanes, in order?

options.text: Methane, ethene, propene and butene
Methane, ethane, propane, pentane
Methane, ethane, butane, octane
Methane, ethane, propane, butane

questions.explanation: These are the first four alkanes named by the specification, in order of increasing carbon number.

questions.stem: What do the molecules in one fraction of crude oil have in common?

options.text: They are all molecules of exactly the same compound
They have a similar number of carbon atoms
They all contain the same number of hydrogen atoms
They all have exactly the same boiling point

questions.explanation: The specification defines a fraction as containing molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms.

questions.stem: An alkane can be shown as a molecular formula or as a displayed formula. What extra information does the displayed formula give?

options.text: It shows the bonds between the atoms
It shows how many atoms there are of each
It shows the charge on each of the atoms
It shows the mass of each atom present

questions.explanation: A displayed formula shows every atom and every covalent bond, which a molecular formula cannot show.

questions.stem: Which of these is a fuel produced from crude oil?

options.text: Charcoal, made by heating wood
Bioethanol, from fermentation
Kerosene, an aircraft fuel
Biodiesel, made from plant oils

questions.explanation: Kerosene is one of the fuels the specification lists as produced from crude oil.
